description: UI Bridge State Machine page — connect to SDK-integrated apps, discover UI states via automated exploration or manual recording with fingerprint-based co-occurrence analysis, then manage state machine configs across seven tabs: Discovery (SDK app connection, explore/record data collection, fingerprint-based state discovery with auto-save), Graph Editor (interactive dagre node-edge layout with element thumbnails, drag-and-drop element reassignment, transition creation), State View (list + spatial + screenshot modes via shared StateViewPanel), Transitions (list with action playback via shared TransitionsPanel), Pathfinding (find optimal paths between states via shared PathfindingPanel), Exploration Results (dashboard with pass rate, coverage stats, discrepancy severity groups, history list, and per-state detail with confidence scores, element verification, and AI analysis prompt), and Export (save to JSON file or load into Python runtime).

groups.name: Page Header and Config Selector
groups.description: The page header shows a Network icon, the active config name (or 'UI Bridge States' when none is selected), and a config selector dropdown with a Refresh button. Users pick an existing config to load it. There is no 'New' or 'Delete' button — configs are created through the Discovery flow.

assertions.description: The page displays the active config name in the header, or 'UI Bridge States' when no config is selected
assertions.precondition: No config is currently selected

assertions.description: Users see a config selector dropdown with a 'Select configuration...' placeholder option to choose which state machine config to work with
A 'Refresh' button reloads the config list and active config. It shows a spinning RefreshCw icon during loading and is disabled with opacity-50 while loading.
When a config is selected, the header title changes from 'UI Bridge States' to show the active config's name
assertions.expected: After selecting a config from the dropdown, the h1 heading should change from 'UI Bridge States' to the selected config's name. Selecting the blank option should revert to 'UI Bridge States'.
assertions.precondition: At least one config exists in the dropdown

groups.name: Tab Navigation Bar
groups.description: Seven tabs appear below the header and are always visible (regardless of config selection): Discovery, Graph Editor, State View, Transitions, Pathfinding, Exploration Results, and Export. The active tab is highlighted with a background shadow. Each tab has an icon and label.

assertions.description: The Discovery tab provides SDK app connection and automated/manual state discovery
The Graph Editor tab provides access to the interactive dagre-based node-edge visualization of states and transitions
The State View tab shows all states with list, spatial, and screenshot view modes
The Transitions tab lists all transitions between states with selection, filtering, and action playback
The Pathfinding tab enables users to find optimal paths between states in the config graph
The Exploration Results tab shows a dashboard with pass rate, coverage stats, discrepancy severity groups, and per-state detail
The Export tab provides JSON file export and runtime loading operations for state machine configs
Exactly 7 tabs are rendered in the tab bar
assertions.expected: The tab bar section below the header should contain exactly 7 tab buttons: Discovery, Graph Editor, State View, Transitions, Pathfinding, Exploration Results, Export

groups.description: The Graph Editor tab renders an interactive node-edge graph using @xyflow/react with dagre layout. States are nodes and transitions are edges. A floating 'Add Transition' button is positioned at top-left. Clicking a node opens the state detail side panel; clicking an edge opens the transition editor side panel. Supports drag-and-drop element reassignment between states and transition deletion. An empty graph shows an instructional message.

assertions.precondition: A config is selected with at least one state, Graph Editor tab is active

groups.name: Discovery Algorithm: Fingerprint-Based State Grouping
groups.description: The state discovery algorithm uses fingerprint-based co-occurrence analysis to group UI elements into states. Co-occurrence data is collected via exploration (automated interaction) or recording (manual capture). Each capture produces a fingerprint of visible interactive elements. States are discovered by clustering fingerprints with similar element sets. The algorithm correctness can be verified by examining the discovered states' element lists and confidence scores.

assertions.description: Every discovered state should have at least one element in its definition. A state with zero elements indicates a grouping error.
assertions.expected: In the discovery results state preview list, each state entry should have associated elements. The state detail (visible after saving and selecting in Graph Editor) should show a non-empty Elements list for every state.
assertions.precondition: Discovery has completed with results

assertions.description: Each discovered state should have a confidence score between 0% and 100%. Higher confidence indicates the state was observed more consistently across captures.
assertions.expected: In the state preview list, each state's confidence should be displayed as '[X]% confidence' where X is between 0 and 100. States with very low confidence (< 30%) may indicate noise in the captured data.
assertions.precondition: Discovery has completed with results

assertions.description: The co-occurrence data summary should show consistent capture and fingerprint counts that match the collection method used
assertions.expected: The data summary card should show: (1) capture count > 0 (matching the presence matrix length), (2) fingerprint count > 0, (3) source badge showing 'via explore' or 'via record' matching the collection method. The capture count should be >= fingerprint count since multiple captures can share a fingerprint.
assertions.precondition: Co-occurrence data has been collected

groups.name: State Model Rules (qontinui/multistate)
groups.description: The state machine follows the multistate model (qontinui/multistate), which extends model-based GUI automation theory. These rules define how states, elements, and screenshots relate to each other. The multistate formal model is Ω = (S, T, G, ω, Td) where S is the set of states, T the transitions, G state groups, ω the occlusion function, and Td dynamic transition generation. All state machine features — discovery, graph editing, state view, screenshots, and export — must conform to these rules. Source: https://qontinui.github.io/multistate/

assertions.description: Multiple states are active simultaneously. The visible screen is described as a set of active states SΞ. A screenshot captures the current screen, which contains elements from multiple co-active states (e.g., a toolbar state, a sidebar state, and a content state all active at once). The same state can be active across many different screens — this is why the same elements appear on multiple pages without belonging to multiple states. States can transition independently without affecting other active states.
assertions.expected: The state machine viewer should support and display multiple co-active states. The screenshot view should show bounding boxes from multiple states simultaneously. State transitions should not force all other states to deactivate.

assertions.description: An image/element belongs to exactly one state. Images do not cross state boundaries. If the same visual element appears on multiple screens, it is because the state that owns it is active on all those screens. The element is not shared across states — it has one owner. This is a fundamental invariant of the model.
assertions.expected: In the graph editor and state view, every element should appear in exactly one state. No element should be listed under multiple states. The discovery algorithm must assign each fingerprint hash to exactly one state.

assertions.description: States are defined through co-occurrence analysis. Elements that always appear together form a state. States are the minimal co-occurring sets derived from observing which elements appear on which screens. Example: images 1,2,3 appear on screens A and B; images 1,2,3,4,5 appear on screens C, D, and E. This produces two states: State 1 owns images 1,2,3 (they co-occur on all 5 screens), State 2 owns images 4,5 (they co-occur only on screens C,D,E). A state is formally a collection of related GUI elements chosen to model a distinct configuration of the user interface.
assertions.expected: Discovered states should contain elements that consistently co-occur across captures. Elements that appear on different subsets of screens should be assigned to different states.

assertions.description: Images signal a state's presence, not its absence. Individual images can reliably confirm a state is active, but a missing image does NOT prove the state is inactive. A state is only deactivated by an explicit transition, never by image disappearance. When a state is active, a specific action performed on one of its objects should give the same expected result every time.
assertions.expected: The state machine should not mark a state as inactive simply because one of its elements was not found. State deactivation should only occur through transition execution.

assertions.description: A screenshot contains elements from whichever states were active at capture time. The elementBoundsJson for a screenshot must contain ONLY the elements that were actually visible on screen when the screenshot was taken. These elements may belong to multiple different co-active states — that is expected. But elements from a page that was NOT being viewed must NOT appear in the screenshot's element data.
assertions.expected: In the Screenshot State View, bounding boxes should only outline elements actually visible in the screenshot image. No bounding boxes should float over blank areas or elements not visually present. Bounding box positions must be actual pixel positions from the capture moment, not averaged or estimated positions.

assertions.description: A screenshot is associated with a state if the state's elements are visible in it. Using the co-occurrence example: State 1 (images 1,2,3) is associated with screenshots from screens A,B,C,D,E. State 2 (images 4,5) is associated with screenshots from screens C,D,E only. A single screenshot will typically match multiple co-active states. A state whose elements were never visible in a screenshot should not match that screenshot.
assertions.expected: In the Screenshot State View, the screenshots column should only show screenshots where the selected state's elements are present. Multiple states matching the same screenshot is expected (co-active states). States from a different page should show no matching screenshots.

assertions.description: Element bounding boxes must be actual pixel positions in their specific screenshot. A bounding box records where the element physically appeared at that specific moment. Averaged positions from co-occurrence statistics or estimated positions from relative viewport percentages are not valid bounding box data for a specific screenshot.
assertions.expected: Bounding boxes on the screenshot canvas should precisely outline the visual elements they represent. The coordinates in elementBoundsJson should come from the actual element bounds at capture time, not from averaged relativePosition data.

assertions.description: When a state opens and obscures another (e.g., a modal dialog over the main window), the covered state is registered as hidden but remains active. The multistate model defines an occlusion function ω: S × S × ℝ → [0,1] that models state visibility. Occlusion is transitive: if s1 occludes s2 and s2 occludes s3, then s1 occludes s3. Blocking states (is_blocking=true) represent modal-like states that prevent interaction with occluded states.
assertions.expected: States marked as blocking should be recognized as modal/overlay states. The graph editor should support the staysVisible transition property for modeling occlusion relationships.

assertions.description: Transitions follow a phased execution model: VALIDATE → OUTGOING → ACTIVATE → INCOMING → EXIT. Activation is a pure memory operation that cannot fail (infallible). If incoming verification fails, the system rolls back to the original state and skips the exit phase. Transitions can activate multiple states atomically and exit multiple states atomically. Each activated state becomes a potential path node for future navigation.
assertions.expected: Transitions in the graph editor should support multiple activate and exit states. The transition detail panel should allow specifying both activate and exit state sets.

groups.name: Observation Pipeline Surface
groups.description: Co-occurrence observations drive state element lists via a derive → promote → invalidate → undo loop. The page surface exposes this via ObservationsPanel (mounted below the page header) and ProvenanceBadge (rendered next to each state name in the detail panel). ObservationsPanel shows the most recent drift fit_score (from GET /state-discovery/drift-scores), offers a 'Re-derive all' bulk action (POST /state-discovery/derive?window_days=90), an 'Invalidate spec observations' button (POST /co-occurrence/invalidate — disabled with tooltip when the StateMachineConfig has no spec_id), and an invalidation log table fed by GET /co-occurrence/invalidations. Each invalidation is grouped by undo_token; rows within the 24 h window show an Undo button (POST /co-occurrence/invalidate/undo). ProvenanceBadge renders three variants — green 'observed' (with support/contrast tooltip + observation count + age), gray 'ai-generated', yellow 'ai-fallback' (with invalidation age). Missing provenance on older compiled SMs silently falls back to 'ai-generated'.

assertions.description: The ObservationsPanel mounts below the page header and shows a 'Drift fit score' label followed by either 'no drift data yet' (fresh runner) or a numeric fit_score with observations_matched/observations_considered and a timestamp.
assertions.expected: Drift fit score

assertions.description: A 'Re-derive all' button appears in the ObservationsPanel header row. Clicking it POSTs /state-discovery/derive (window_days=90), persists a state_discovery_artifact row, and shows a toast 'Derived N states from M observations' on success. While in flight, the button shows a spinner and is disabled.

An 'Invalidate spec observations' button appears next to 'Re-derive all'. When the active StateMachineConfig has a spec_id it is clickable and POSTs /co-occurrence/invalidate with that spec_id. When spec_id is absent (known gap: StateMachineConfig has no spec_id column yet) the button is disabled; its title tooltip reads 'Spec has no spec_id — invalidation-all is disabled'.

The ObservationsPanel renders an 'Invalidation log' heading. On a fresh runner the table shows 'No invalidations recorded for this spec.' Populated rows show columns When / Reason / By / Fingerprints / Action. Rows are grouped by undo_token so a single invalidate call producing N observation rows collapses into one log entry with summed fingerprints_count.
assertions.expected: Invalidation log

assertions.description: When GET /co-occurrence/invalidations returns an empty array for the current spec, the log shows exactly 'No invalidations recorded for this spec.' rather than an empty table. This prevents ambiguity between 'still loading' and 'nothing to show'.
assertions.expected: No invalidations recorded for this spec.
assertions.precondition: No invalidations have been emitted for this spec within the current window

assertions.description: Each invalidation log row within 24 h of invalidated_at shows an 'Undo' action button. Clicking it POSTs /co-occurrence/invalidate/undo with the row's undo_token; the backend enforces the 24 h window via 'invalidated_at > now() - interval 24 hours' so expired undo tokens no-op server-side. On success the row is cleared from the log on next refresh and the observation_count used by /state-discovery/derive returns to its pre-invalidate value.
assertions.precondition: At least one invalidation exists within the 24 h window

assertions.description: When a state's compiled provenance is 'observed' (promoted from accumulated co-occurrence observations with support ≥ 0.75 and contrast ≥ 0.10), a green pill renders next to the state name in the State View detail panel. Its text reads 'observed' followed by '· N obs' (observationCount) and an age of the last_observed timestamp. Hovering surfaces a tooltip with the full support/contrast numbers.
assertions.precondition: At least one compiled state has provenance='observed' in stateMachine.states[].provenance

assertions.description: States authored from the spec JSON (or predating the provenance field) render a gray 'ai-generated' pill. Missing/undefined provenance falls back to this variant silently so older compiled SMs don't regress. The badge never throws or renders empty.

When a state was previously 'observed' but its observations were invalidated within the last 24 h, the compiler emits provenance='ai-fallback'. The badge renders yellow with text 'ai-fallback' plus an 'invalidated <Nh ago>' age from provenanceMeta.invalidatedAt. This signals the model is rebuilding from scratch — the JSON-authored element list is in use until re-derivation re-accumulates support above threshold.
assertions.precondition: At least one state in the compiled SM was invalidated in the last 24 h

assertions.description: POST /state-discovery/derive returns an artifact whose states[] is the clustering of observation fingerprints via qontinui.discovery.discover_states_from_renders. The number of states shown in the response must equal the number of distinct element-set configurations in the observation window — not one per observation. A 3-observation run over a single page must produce exactly one state, not three. Repeated calls on the same observation set must produce the same state-hash set (input-order pinned by captured_at,id).

Observed or ai-fallback states must satisfy the one-state-per-element invariant: no fingerprint may appear in more than one state's element list simultaneously. Violations cause compile-state-machine.ts to THROW (not just warn). For provenance='ai-generated' states the compiler downgrades to console.warn — they're sketches and may share elements until observations accumulate.
